seo.title: Karmic tail 15 8 11 compatibility: the riddle of the lion and honey
seo.description: Karmic tail 15 8 11 compatibility: The Devil at the entry, Justice in the middle, Strength as the main task, and why its plot is written in the Book of Judges.

title: Karmic tail 15-8-11 in compatibility: The Devil, Justice and Strength
short: At his own wedding Samson put a riddle to the guests: "Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness." The answer was bees and honey in the carcass of a lion he had torn apart with his bare hands. The karmic tail 15-8-11 in a couple's compatibility asks the two of them the same riddle: how to make sweetness come out of their strength, rather than a defeated partner.

sections.h2: Tail to tail: how a couple's 15-8-11 is formed
paragraphs: The same story holds the most literal picture of a couple's tail there is. Wronged by his father-in-law, Samson "caught three hundred foxes, and took firebrands, and turned tail to tail, and put a firebrand in the midst between two tails" (Judges 15:4). A couple's tail is made the same way: neither partner brings it, it is tied together from two personal tails. Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, reduced to 22.

An example: a couple born on 05.12.1976 and 05.07.1975. The first partner's personal tail is 3-7-22, the second's is 12-19-7. Entries are added to entries, middles to middles, main tasks to main tasks:

The couple's middle is counted from the two personal middles, not from the couple's outer numbers. Here the two happen to agree (15 + 11 = 26 → 8), but that is a result, not a method. This couple's centre is 13, Death (8 + 5), and the couple's values are 12, The Hanged Man.

Now the first clue. The couple's tail 15-8-11 arises from five combinations of personal tails, and in all five the entries are 3 and 12 or 6 and 9. Neither partner has a fifteen at the entry of their own tail: the couple's Devil is born only between them, like a firebrand tied between two tails. Nobody brings the wish to hold the other whole into the union — it appears when the two meet.
The rest also comes from checking every date:

ul: the tail occurs in about one couple in 120 (0.834%), ranking 43rd of the 97 couple tails;
in 65% of such couples the partners' personal tails are 12-19-7 and 3-7-22, as in the example;
in 21% they are 6-17-11 and 9-9-18: one partner already has Strength as the main task of their own tail, and the couple's task sounds familiar to them;
in 11% they are 6-5-17 and 9-3-21; two more combinations give about one per cent each.

paragraphs: No other couple tail is made of these numbers. The first number of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, so 8 and 11 cannot stand at the entry, and the order 15-11-8 never comes up across all dates. 15-8-11 is the only one.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Devil: "wherewith thou mightest be bound"
paragraphs: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, its "common language". In this tail the common language is the language of the tether. Delilah speaks it in her very first line: "Tell me, I pray thee, wherein thy great strength lieth, and wherewith thou mightest be bound to afflict thee" (16:6).

What follows is usually retold as betrayal, though at first the text reads more like a game. Samson answers: seven green withs. She binds him and cries "The Philistines be upon thee, Samson" — and he breaks the withs "as a thread of tow is broken when it toucheth the fire". Then new ropes. Then seven locks woven into the web. Three times she binds him, three times he breaks free — and he does not leave. The text does not say why, but the game repeats, and both play it: one binds, the other shows he can break the bonds. As long as it is a game, the ropes snap like thread.

This is what The Devil at the entry looks like in ordinary life. The two are pulled towards each other with a force that would do for ten. Jealousy is taken for proof of love, "where were you?" for care. Each wants to know everything about the other and keeps testing whether the knot still holds. In Lisovskaya this is both the energy's plus — passion, readiness to accept the partner's dark sides, open talk about desires — and its minus: only closeness holds the couple together, one presses while the other keeps quiet about what they want, and people are held by the body, by money, by a child, by status. The entry stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can turn into resistance: the harder they hold, the harder they pull away.

There is a detail that is easy to miss. Samson is a Nazarite from birth, and the Nazarite law forbids him anything from the vine (Numbers 6:3–4). Yet he loves a woman "in the valley of Sorek" — and in Hebrew soreq means "choice vine" (the same word names the choicest vine in Isaiah 5:2 and the noble vine in Jeremiah 2:21). He meets the lion by the vineyards of Timnath, and his foxes with their firebrands burn the corn along with the vineyards. He is always drawn to where he is not allowed to go. That is the entry of The Devil: a desire that grows stronger the less it is permitted.

Why bind at all? The Bible does not explain; Milton did. In his drama Samson Agonistes (1671) Dalila is no longer a lover but Samson's wife, and her visit to her blinded husband in prison reads like a marital quarrel. She says what the Book of Judges never does: she "feared lest one day thou wouldst leave me / As her at Timna". She knew that liberty "Would draw thee forth to perilous enterprises, / While I at home sate full of cares and fears". Here he would be with her day and night — "Mine and Love's prisoner, not the Philistines', / Whole to myself". Beneath the wish to bind lies the fear of being left. Among the tasks of the fifteenth energy Lisovskaya lists exactly this: fear, and attempts to hold on.

Samson's reply is half a line, and the way out of this entry rests on it: "Love seeks to have love." And one more line: "This gaol I count the house of liberty / To thine whose doors my feet shall never enter." If the wish to hold goes unseen, home becomes a cage, and a prison cell feels freer.

An important caveat. In the story one partner betrays and the other is betrayed. In a couple's tail that never happens: there is one tail for two. Samson binds too — the foxes tail to tail, the wedding guests with a wager of thirty garments — and he hides things too: he told not even his father and mother about the lion and the honey. The tail does not say which partner is Samson and which is Delilah, and gender has nothing to do with it. Each asks "what can I bind you with?", and each hides a lock of their own.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — Justice: "thou hast mocked me these three times"
paragraphs: The middle of the task is how the couple lives the road from the wish to the main task. Here the road runs across the scales. Delilah keeps count out loud: "Behold, thou hast mocked me, and told me lies", "Hitherto thou hast mocked me", and finally: "How canst thou say, I love thee, when thine heart is not with me? thou hast mocked me these three times" (16:10–15). Love has become a ledger: you say "I love thee" — show me your heart. Samson answers the count in his own way: three times he invents new bonds.

Two chapters earlier the same scene has already played out, in almost the same words. His wife from Timnath weeps: "Thou dost but hate me, and lovest me not: thou hast put forth a riddle unto the children of my people, and hast not told it me." Samson answers by his own measure: "Behold, I have not told it my father nor my mother, and shall I tell it thee?" (14:16). Two ledgers: in hers, closeness is proved by a secret; in his, my parents come before you. The women differ, the quarrel is the same. This is how the middle of the tail works: the same account keeps coming back until it is settled differently.

And there is one more detail that makes the skin crawl. While Delilah binds Samson, "there were men lying in wait, abiding with her in the chamber" (16:9, 16:12). In every test there is someone else, out of sight. A couple has such a third party too — a mother who "always said so", a friend, an ex whose opinion matters. The ledger is kept not for the two of them but for whoever is sitting behind the curtain. Among Lisovskaya's recommendations for Justice is to set limits on advice and help from others.

Samson in this story is not just a strongman — he is a judge. "And he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years" (15:20), and again in the very last line (16:31). Yet the story does not show a single case he judged. His justice is a mirror: "As they did unto me, so have I done unto them" (15:11); "Now shall I be more blameless than the Philistines, though I do them a displeasure" (15:3). Benebell Wen describes reversed Justice almost as this plot: "actions that may be unjust rather than just", "prompted by the Seeker's feeling that what happened was not fair".

In a couple this looks peaceful, but recognisable. "I told you everything — and you?" "Last time it was me who gave in." "We always visit your parents, never mine." Honesty turns into an instrument of control, responsibility into pressure. Among the minuses of Justice Lisovskaya names over-responsibility that slides into control, the habit of measuring everyone by oneself, and the inability to admit one's own fault. Among the pluses: a fair share of duties, promises kept, "a cool head and a warm heart". And among the tasks of the eight she names forgiveness.

In Milton the argument over forgiveness is the heart of the whole scene. Dalila asks for her offence to be weighed "By itself, with aggravations not surcharged, / Or else with just allowance counterpoised". Then she makes an offer that is hard to call unfair: "Let weakness then with weakness come to parle, / So near related, or the same of kind; / Thine forgive mine". She reminds him that he himself gave the secret away under pressure, and asks him not to exact "More strength from me than in thyself was found". Samson answers with perfect justice: take for your deed exactly the pardon I give my own folly — "Impartial, self-severe, inexorable". One measure for both, and therefore no mercy at all.

That is the trap in the middle of the tail. Justice in the minus is not necessarily deceit or counting in one's own favour. More often it is an honest ledger without forgiveness: "I don't forgive myself either, so don't expect it." The scales are the middle of the road; one cannot settle down and live on them.

sections.h2: Main task — Strength: a lion that need not be torn
paragraphs: The couple's main task is read mostly through its minus — what does not work out and what has to be learned. From the first scene Samson's strength is a strength that tears. A young lion "roared against him", and Samson "rent him as he would have rent a kid, and he had nothing in his hand" (14:6). Then the gates of Gaza, posts, bar and all, on his shoulders. Then the jawbone of an ass. Not once does his strength become gentle, and it never comes by his choice: "the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him" — so begin the lion, Ashkelon and Lehi (14:6, 14:19, 15:14). Strength overtakes him like a storm.

Delilah's question "wherein thy great strength lieth" is the very question of the main task. In the Hebrew one and the same verb stands behind it three times, and the King James Bible keeps it each time: the lords want "to bind him to afflict him" (16:5), Delilah asks what will bind him "to afflict thee" (16:6), and after the shaving "she began to afflict him" (16:19). The Russian Synodal Bible renders the last of these as "and he began to weaken" — and takes the verb out of her hands. In the original, strength in this story is a thing that can be taken away: find the secret, shave it off, bind it.

This is what the minus of the eleventh energy looks like in a couple, according to Lisovskaya: a struggle for leadership, suppression and fear, each with their own truth, mockery of the other's weakness. Strength is either hidden like a weapon or someone tries to worm it out and disarm it. And the strongest man has a fear he repeats from answer to answer: "then shall I be weak, and be as another man". What he fears is not pain but becoming ordinary. For a couple with Strength as the main task this fear is familiar: to show the other your weakness, because it can be used.

Benebell Wen opens the Strength card with the words "Triumph of love over hate" — and goes on: "the Seeker cannot use brute force to exercise will over others; the Seeker must use gentle, subtle influence." Both of Samson's women speak to him about hate: "Thou dost but hate me, and lovest me not." Milton's Dalila turns this around: "And what if love, which thou interpret'st hate, / The jealousy of love… / Caused what I did?" The task of Strength in this tail is to tell love from hate where they speak in the same words. Reversed Strength Wen describes as reliance on brute force and as being "too stubborn and obstinate".

The most important sentence in Judges for this tail is 16:20. Shaven, Samson wakes and says: "I will go out as at other times before, and shake myself." The old way — breaking the bonds — no longer works. "And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him." His strength left not with his hair but with the broken vow: the secret was not a mechanism but a promise. For a couple this is the main key: the strength of a union lies not in what each hides from the other, but in what both keep.

And finally the scene in which the whole task of the tail can be seen. Milton's Dalila asks: "Let me approach at least, and touch thy hand." Samson: "Not for thy life, lest fierce remembrance wake / My sudden rage to tear thee joint by joint. / At distance I forgive thee, go with that." He tore a lion apart in his youth, and now the lion sits inside him, and he can forgive only at a distance, because up close the lion would break loose. Just before this Dalila tells him: "If thou in strength all mortals dost exceed, / In uncompassionate anger do not so."

The main task of 15-8-11 is the reverse of "at distance I forgive thee". To let a hand come near one's lion and not tear it. To stay close while the anger has not yet passed. Lisovskaya puts it in everyday words: work with aggression, learn mutual respect, say from the very start what you like and what you don't, express feelings openly. Milton himself, incidentally, knew this choice not only from books: his first wife, Mary Powell, left him for her mother soon after their wedding in 1642, came back in 1645 — and he took her in. His Samson forgives at a distance; the poet himself forgave up close.

sections.h2: What Waite's cards show: fire on the tail and a hand at the jaws
paragraphs: The pictures here are those of the classic Waite–Smith deck; the cards on this site are drawn differently. But Waite's three cards read like illustrations to the Book of Judges.

**The Devil.** Two tailed figures are chained to a ring by the altar, and above them stands a horned figure with a torch pointing down to the earth. Benebell Wen notices what most people pass over: the torch "appears to be lighting the primordial man's tail on fire", while "the female figure's tail bears fruit" (in the picture, a bunch of grapes). Fire on a tail and the vine — exactly Samson's foxes: a firebrand between two tails, let loose into the standing corn, burned the vineyards and the olives too. There are two chains on the card, and in Gaza Samson was "bound with fetters of brass" (16:21; the Hebrew uses the dual, "a pair of bronzes"). In Waite's divinatory list the reversed Devil includes "weakness" and "blindness", and Samson in the prison house is both weak and blind.

**Justice.** A figure with a sword and scales sits between two pillars. The last scene of Samson the judge is between pillars too: "they set him between the pillars" (16:25), and he takes hold of "the two middle pillars upon which the house stood". His last prayer is about settling a score: "that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes". A judge who spent his life settling scores settles the last one at the end and brings the house down with himself inside. A couple knows this in a peaceful form: a quarrel in which the aim is not to agree but to bring the score to zero loosens the pillars of the shared home.

**Strength.** A woman holds her hands at a lion's jaws, and the lion does not resist. This is exactly the scene missing from Samson's story: his lion is either torn apart or sits inside him and roars "at distance". In Waite's divinatory list Strength has "Power, energy, action, courage, magnanimity", and reversed Strength has, among other things, "abuse of power, weakness, discord, sometimes even disgrace". Samson came to know disgrace at the end: he was fetched from prison so that he might "make us sport" at the feast. The word "weakness" stands in Waite's lists for both the reversed Devil and reversed Strength: the most famous strongman of the Bible spends the whole story afraid of becoming weak, and weak is what he becomes. (In Waite's deck Strength and Justice swap numbers; on this site 8 is Justice and 11 is Strength.)

sections.h2: The couple's centre and values: honey in the carcass of a lion
paragraphs: The couple's centre is the atmosphere inside the union, what lies between two people and is not for show. In three couples out of four with this tail (76.4%) the centre is 13, Death. This is not about anyone dying. Waite writes of the thirteenth card as "change, transformation and passage from lower to higher". In Lisovskaya the atmosphere of Death in the plus is accepting the partner's past and moving on, taking changes in each other easily; in the minus, emotional swings and attempts to remake the other.

With Samson's riddle this fits literally. "Out of the eater came forth meat": the one who ate became food, and the honey was found where the lion was already dead. For sweetness to appear in a couple, something in it has to end — an old form of strength, the duel, the game of who binds whom. The guests' answer to Samson — "What is sweeter than honey? and what is stronger than a lion?" — has long been read by scholars as a second riddle. The German biblical scholar Hermann Stahn suggested in 1908 that it was a wedding riddle whose answer was "love"; among the other answers proposed is "death". Both answers meet in a single verse: "for love is strong as death" (Song of Songs 8:6).

In 21.4% of couples the centre is 22, The Fool: an atmosphere of lightness, freedom and play. Samson plays too — he wagers garments on a riddle, he lets himself be bound. The Fool makes the game of the tether lighter and more dangerous: in the minus it becomes a relationship as a game, with no boundaries and no responsibility. In 2.2% the centre is 4, The Emperor — order and authority, when "who is in charge" is settled by rules.

The couple's values are what the union exists for. In 41.7% they are 12, The Hanged Man. In prison, at the darkest point of the story, there is a quiet verse: "Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven" (16:22). Waite calls The Hanged Man "life in suspension, but life and not death". The value of such a couple is a pause in which what was cut off grows back, and the ability to look at one's own strength from the other side. In 31.9% of couples the values are 21, The World: wholeness, a shared outlook, accepting the partner even in the minus. In 26.4% they are 3, The Empress: fruitfulness, home, plenty — the honey itself. In the example above the centre is Death, the values are The Hanged Man, and Strength also stands on the point "What fills": what the couple is learning is also what restores it.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail: out of the strong came forth sweetness
paragraphs: Since 1885 the tins of Britain's Lyle's Golden Syrup have shown a lion with bees above it and the words "Out of the strong came forth sweetness". In 2006 Guinness World Records named it the world's oldest branding and packaging. Samson's riddle has stood on kitchen shelves for almost a century and a half as a sign of sweetness. But the lion on the tin is dead. The tail 15-8-11 asks about another version: can honey be had from a living lion?

The strong version of the tail looks like this. Passion stays passion but does not become a cage: "love seeks to have love", not a prisoner. Secrets are told by choice, not on the seventh day of tears. The ledger is kept, but there is one for both, with a column marked "forgiven". Strength and weakness are shown to each other before anyone has to ask "wherein thy great strength lieth". And forgiveness does not come from a distance.
What helps a couple through this tail:

ul: not prying: a secret extracted under pressure brings no closeness, it becomes evidence;
noticing when "I love thee" starts being tested with "thine heart is not with me";
asking who else is "abiding in the chamber" during a quarrel — whose opinion, whose voice, whose ledger;
not settling scores at the peak of anger, and not mistaking justice for punishment;
speaking of one's own "lock" — the vulnerable place — oneself, rather than waiting for it to be found;
moving closer when the urge is to forgive from a distance.

paragraphs: If there are threats, physical violence or fear for one's safety in a couple, that is not "the task of the tail" and not a reason to put up with it. It is a reason to call for help: a local emergency number, a crisis line, a psychologist.

Samson's guests answered his riddle with a question: "What is sweeter than honey? and what is stronger than a lion?" A couple with the tail 15-8-11 answers it not in words but in the way they live: when the strength of two stops being a duel, out of the strong comes forth sweetness.

ul: **15 · The Devil — entry to the task.** What draws the couple together is the wish to hold each other whole: passion, jealous closeness, the very question Delilah puts to Samson — "wherewith thou mightest be bound".
**8 · Justice — middle of the task.** The road runs through a ledger: who opened up, gave and forgave how much. "How canst thou say, I love thee, when thine heart is not with me?"
**11 · Strength — main task.** To learn a strength that needs neither to bind nor to hide: to come close to the other's "lion" and not tear it apart.

intro: This is not a verdict and not a forecast. The tail describes a road the couple walks together, and the Book of Judges records that road almost word for word — from a riddle at a wedding to a prison in Gaza.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 15-8-11 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of the couple's chart: **The Devil** at the entry to the task, **Justice** in the middle, **Strength** as the main task. The couple is drawn together by a strong wish to hold each other, the road runs through a ledger of openness and grievances, and the main task is strength without a struggle for power: a closeness in which nothing needs to be bound and nothing vulnerable needs to be hidden.

faq.q: Is the couple's tail 15-8-11 a bad sign for a relationship?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not grade the union and predicts nothing: it shows what the two have to learn. The Devil at the entry is both passion and the risk of jealous possession; Justice is both fair agreements and the counting of grievances; Strength is both respect and a struggle for leadership. Which side shows depends on what the couple does.

faq.q: How is the couple's tail 15-8-11 different from the personal tail 15-8-11?
faq.a: The personal tail 15-8-11 is calculated from a single date of birth and read through the roles of a personal chart. In a couple each point is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, and the roles are different: the entry to the task, the middle, and the couple's main task. Even with the same numbers it is a different calculation, and conclusions about a person do not carry over to a couple.

faq.q: How can a couple find out whether they have the tail 15-8-11?
faq.a: Enter both dates of birth in the compatibility calculator: the tail appears in the sphere "The couple's karmic tail". Most often it is formed from the personal tails 12-19-7 and 3-7-22, but other combinations occur too, for example 6-17-11 and 9-9-18.

faq.q: Can a couple's tail have the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. From the numbers 15, 8 and 11 a couple can only get the order 15-8-11: the first number of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, and the order 15-11-8 never comes up across all dates.

faq.q: What should a couple with the tail 15-8-11 do?
faq.a: Speak about their wishes and fears directly instead of testing each other; keep one honest ledger for both and forgive up close, not from a distance; never settle who is in charge by force. If there are threats or violence in the relationship, help is needed: a local emergency number, a crisis line, a psychologist.

report: Samson put a riddle to the guests at his own wedding: "Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness." A couple with the tail 15-8-11 faces the same riddle, only it is put to two people: how to make sweetness come out of their strength, rather than a defeated partner. The Book of Judges records the road to the answer almost word for word, in three lines of dialogue.

report.h3: The first line: "wherewith thou mightest be bound"

This is The Devil at the entry to the task — what the couple wants together. Its common language is the language of the tether. not settling scores at the peak of anger, and not mistaking justice for punishment;
speaking of one's own "lock" — the vulnerable place — oneself, rather than waiting for it to be found.

report: If there are threats, physical violence or fear for one's safety in a couple, that is not "the task of the tail" and not a reason to put up with it. It is a reason to call for help: a local emergency number, a crisis line, a psychologist.

unit.title: Honey from a living lion

captions.M: Wanting to hold each other whole
captions.N: Passing through the ledger, not living on the scales
captions.D: Letting a hand near your lion and not tearing it

unit.meaning: Your task is not to bind each other, to keep one ledger for both and to forgive while staying close, not from a distance.
